---
title: "Running the workflows"
subtitle: "The four entry points, the wrapper, and the flags that matter"
---

The four `*.smk` files at the repository root are the only entry points. There
is no package CLI: you invoke Snakemake against a workflow and a config.

| Entry point | id | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `analyze_climate.smk` | wf0 | The basin's historical climate — **model-free** |
| `build_model.smk` | wf1 | Builds the Wflow-SBM model, runs it on historical forcing |
| `analyze_projections.smk` | wf2 | CMIP6 change factors — a plausibility overlay |
| `run_stress_test.smk` | wf3 | The stress test |

Run them in order; `run_stress_test` needs what `build_model` produced.

## Invoking one workflow

```bash
pixi shell
snakemake all -c 3 -s build_model.smk --configfile test_case/snake_config_rapid.yml
```

The flags worth knowing:

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-s` | which workflow file to run |
| `--configfile` | the YAML configuration |
| `-c` | cores; more than 1 enables parallelism |
| `--dry-run`, `-n` | list what would execute, run nothing |
| `--unlock` | clear the working-directory lock left by a crash |
| `--keep-going`, `-k` | keep running independent jobs after a failure |
| `--notemp` | keep intermediate files Snakemake would delete |

The full option set is in the [Snakemake CLI
documentation](https://snakemake.readthedocs.io/en/stable/executing/cli.html).

The recommended sequence for any workflow is: render the graph, clear a stale
lock if there is one, then run.

```bash
python scripts/plot_workflow_dag.py -s build_model.smk --configfile <config>
snakemake --unlock -s build_model.smk --configfile <config>
snakemake all -c 3 -s build_model.smk --configfile <config>
```

The first command renders a DAG image into `<project_dir>/logs/dag/`, named
after the run that would produce it (`<project_name>_wf<N>_dag.png`, with the
stress test carrying its experiment id). It draws the graph and runs nothing;
it needs Graphviz's `dot`, which the pixi environment provides.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Dry-run after editing anything structural

`--dry-run` validates the whole dependency graph in seconds. Run it after
changing a rule, a script signature, or any config key that feeds a rule's
inputs — it is the difference between finding a broken path now and finding it
forty minutes into a model build.
:::

## Running everything the config enables

`scripts/run_workflows.py` reads the `workflows.<name>.enabled` flags and runs
Snakemake for exactly the enabled workflows, in order:

```bash
pixi run run-workflows --config test_case/snake_config_rapid.yml
pixi run run-workflows --config <config> --cores 4 -- --dry-run
```

What it guarantees:

- It accepts **full-orchestration configs only** — a `workflows:` section with
  all four subsections, each with an `enabled:` key.
- A missing section or key is a **hard error naming the absent key**, never a
  silent default.
- It **stops at the first nonzero Snakemake exit and returns that code**, so a
  failed upstream workflow is never followed by a downstream run.
- `--cores N`, and anything after a `--` sentinel, forwards to every invocation.
- Every invocation — including a dry run, a no-op, or a failure — writes an
  immutable manifest under `<project_dir>/config/runs/invocations/`.

It narrates its own run: which project, which config, a numbered sequence of the
enabled workflows, a line at each workflow's start and finish with its duration,
and a closing verdict listing what was written. Every line it speaks is bounded
by a full-width rule that nothing else in the console draws, so you can always
tell the runner's voice from the workflow's.

::: {.callout-note}
## Run the pipeline from one checkout

Snakemake keeps its "what is up to date" bookkeeping in a `.snakemake/`
directory under the *working directory*, and it locks that directory while
running. Driving one `project_dir` from two checkouts gives you two
disagreeing sets of bookkeeping and two independent locks over the same output
files. Pick one checkout for runs and stay in it.
:::

## Re-running an experiment after a model rebuild

An experiment records the Wflow model it was run against, and the workflow
**refuses to re-run it if that model has changed** — otherwise new model state
would be mixed into old results.

Expect this refusal after *any* rebuild, including one that changed nothing
numeric: the forcing file is not byte-reproducible, because HydroMT varies the
internal chunk layout between writes while the values stay identical.

Read what the error names before deciding:

- **Only `forcing/inmaps_historical.nc` changed** — the known layout-only case.
  Delete the experiment's `config/model_reference.yml` and let the next run
  regenerate it.
- **Anything else is named** — `staticmaps.nc`, `wflow_sbm.toml`, or the forcing
  alongside them — the guard has found something real. Do not re-record. Create a
  new experiment: the recorded one is not re-runnable against different physics
  or state.

Re-recording the reference is an operator decision, not a chore. It means *"this
experiment now accepts the rebuilt model."* A re-record that becomes routine is
how genuine drift eventually gets waved through.
